overview: This broad label follows early Magyar communities from the eastern European steppe into the Carpathian Basin and the emerging Kingdom of Hungary. The map’s 700 start is not a known founding date. Its 900 outline remains misleadingly far east despite settlement in the Carpathian Basin beginning in the late ninth century. These changing communities were ancestors of later Hungarians, not a people who disappeared in 1100.

periods.title: Eastern European backgrounds
periods.summary: The map begins during a complex period of migration and community formation, before settlement in the Carpathian Basin.

periods.title: Settlement and a new kingdom
periods.summary: Settlement was followed by political and religious changes, including a Christian kingdom around the year 1000.

items.text: The late ninth-century movement into the Carpathian Basin was part of a longer history of changing alliances and communities. Researchers debate its stages and earlier geography. The familiar date 895 is a useful landmark, rather than the birthday of an entire people.

Early Magyar life included farming as well as horses. Archaeological and historical research describes people familiar with ploughs and with growing wheat, barley and millet. Settling households could combine crops and livestock, so imagining everyone constantly galloping across the steppe misses much of the work.

Trade linked settlements to distant markets. Arab silver coins help trace northeastern connections, while tenth-century accounts place Magyar traders at Prague and the lower Danube. Goods included horses, silver, furs and weapons. Enslaved people were also traded, a reminder that commercial connections could involve severe human suffering.

At Edelény-Borsod, houses destroyed by fire preserved objects where their owners had used them. The museum describes tenth-century households with about 12 to 16 pottery vessels. Pots, bowls shaped rather like flowerpots and occasional bottles provide a small inventory of everyday equipment.

Some overturned pots at the same settlement contained charred food. Researchers identified millet porridge with meat and, in smaller pots, wild-fruit remains resembling jam. An accidentally burnt dinner became evidence that survived for a thousand years. It does not tell us what every household ate every day.

Ribbed-neck pots from tenth- and eleventh-century Halimba offer another kitchen clue. The museum associates this vessel type with processing and storing milk. That use is an interpretation of the objects, rather than a surviving instruction label saying “put the milk here”.

A study of teeth and bones from tenth-century Kenézlő-Fazekaszug found a diet largely based on plants, with some animal protein. Differences between childhood and adult tissues help researchers investigate changes during life. The results describe this cemetery sample; they are not a menu for all early Hungarians.

Women rode horses too. Female graves sometimes contain riding equipment, and some children were also buried with horse gear. At Soltszentimre, carved bone plates decorated a wealthy woman’s wooden saddle. The museum’s reconstructed saddle shows how surviving pieces may once have fitted together.

The decorated pouch plate from Tiszabezdéd combines twisting plants, two fantastic creatures and a central cross. It is made of gilded copper. Such objects show craftspeople selecting and combining visual ideas from different cultural connections, then fitting them onto something small enough to wear.

Some women wore decorated discs attached to ribbons braided into their hair. Surviving examples include plant patterns and imaginary animals, made in different metalworking techniques. Hair could carry an elaborate display of skilled work, although these rich ornaments cannot stand for everyone’s wardrobe.

Iron stirrups gave riders a place for their feet. Craftspeople decorated some with silver or copper hammered into cut grooves. A museum study also connects broad, curved footrests with soft-soled footwear. Even a practical riding tool can preserve clues about both metalworking and shoes.

The original 1055 charter founding Tihany Abbey is mostly Latin, but includes Hungarian words. A scholarly transcription reads “feheruuaru rea meneh hodu utu rea”: “to the military road leading to Fehérvár”. This is early Hungarian written in Latin letters, from the Christian kingdom after the migration period. It describes a route in a property boundary.

ending.text: The creation of a Christian kingdom around 1000 changed political institutions and religious life. Magyar communities continued within Hungary. The map’s 1100 endpoint closes this label’s coverage, not the history of the people.
